yugen: Yugen is the beauty you feel before you can explain it. A long hooded robe in deep mustard, hand-printed down every edge. Pull the hood up and the street goes quiet. Wear it open over black and let it move.
mani: Mani means jewel, and this one does not whisper. Saffron orange with gold sprigs woven through and a pink border at the hem. It catches every light in the room. Throw it over anything plain and you are dressed.
midori: Haritha is the colour of things that grow slowly. A long sleeveless layer in linen, striped with brown teeth on cream. No sleeves, no fuss, all line. It turns a white tee and trousers into an outfit with a spine.
maitri: Maitri means loving-kindness. It looks like a warning. Black rayon, covered in off-white marks drawn by hand: arrows, houses, bars. Belt it shut or leave it open. Either way people read you before you say a word.
padma: Padma is the lotus: it comes up through mud and stays clean. A short wrap robe in purple stars, tied at the waist with a patterned band. Soft enough for a slow morning, sharp enough to wear out the door.
surya: Surya is the sun, and this is the piece that proves it. A short jacket in sea green, cream flowers all over, a blue band of suns down the front. Cut boxy. Wear it like a shirt you forgot to button.
shunya: Shunya means zero: the empty place where everything starts. A pink block-printed layer with a fringed hem, every square stamped slightly differently. Loose collar, open front. It is the easiest thing here to put on and the hardest to take off.
hikari: Prakasha means light, the first kind, at dawn. A long open robe in brick red on cream, triangles and crossed squares running its full length. It moves when you walk. Stand still and it still looks like motion.
qing: Taruni means a young woman who already knows. A long slip dress in burnt rust, pleated so it shifts as you move. Thin straps, deep neckline, nothing extra. Add boots and a jacket and it stops being a summer dress.
kavya: Kavya means poetry. This is the short kind. A long cream dress with thin straps and rows of raised texture running across it. Quiet from far away, detailed up close. It does not ask for attention and gets it anyway.
dolma: Tara is she who saves. A long ivory dress cut in tiers, each one finished with a soft fringe that moves on its own. Thin straps, deep V. It reads gentle until you wear it with heavy boots.
soma: Soma is the nectar of the moon. A long white dress, blue-green trim running down the front like water, open at the back. Cool on the skin and close to weightless. Made for heat, late nights and bare shoulders.
yeshe: Prajna means wisdom, the kind you earn. A short cream dress with wide flared sleeves, laced at the chest and stitched along every hem. Textured cotton, a little raw. It dresses up without ever looking like it tried.
darvish: Mishra means mixed, and it is: paisley, flowers and panels in turquoise, red and orange, all at once. A long robe-dress that wraps and ties. Nothing else you own will match it. That is the reason to own it.
milarepa: Milarepa was the seeker who gave everything up. This kept the good part. A short white wrap dress in soft cotton, flutter sleeves, diamonds stitched along the edges. Ties at the waist. Light, clean and a little bit sharp.
yashodhara: Yashodhara held her ground in silence. A long halter dress in plum, printed with rows of fans laid like scales. It hangs straight from the neck and moves from the hip. The back is bare. The rest is yours.
indra: Indra rules the heavens. This rules a wardrobe. A long-sleeved top in deep plum, buttoned at the neck and gathered at the front. The colour does the work. Tuck it in, leave it loose, or wear it open as a layer.
vajra: Vajra means thunderbolt. An off-shoulder tee in crepe cotton, cut crooked on purpose, with one triangle pocket. One shoulder out, one hem low. It looks wrong on a hanger and right on a body. That is the point.
tian: Svarga means sky. A short-sleeved tee in open net, cream shot through with yellow, so skin and light both come through. Wear it alone when it is hot. Layer it over black when you want it to show.
satya: Satya means truth. A pale blue shirt in soft linen, cut loose with a real collar and nothing to hide behind. It creases, and it should. Sleeves down, sleeves rolled, open over a tee. It works every way.
rei: Anugraha means grace. A cropped white tee in crepe cotton with raw edges and a triangle pocket. Short in the body, wide in the sleeve. The simplest piece in the collection and the one you will wear most.
dao: Dao means the way. A striped cotton shirt in pale blue and white, cut straight and easy. Cool against the skin, crisp at the collar. Wear it buttoned to the top or open to the waist. No wrong turn.
tenzin: Dharin means the one who holds. A white hooded pullover in soft linen, laced at the neck, loose everywhere else. Hood up, it is shelter. Hood down, it is the cleanest thing in the room. Roomy enough to layer under.
yun: Megha means cloud. Wrap trousers in deep red that cross at the front and fall wide to the ankle. They tie, so they fit. They swing, so they get noticed. Every step shows a little more than the last.
rinchen: Amulya means priceless. Draped trousers in soft cotton, striped grey on white, gathered low and loose through the leg. They move like water and sit like nothing else you own. Pair them with something fitted on top.
amara-1: Nidra means deep sleep, and they feel like it. Wrap-front trousers in sand, layered over themselves and cut relaxed. Dressed down they are loungewear. With a shirt tucked in, they are the smartest thing you will wear all week.
aiko: Priya means beloved. Trousers in deep green, cream teeth running down each leg between fine stripes. Loud in the best way. Keep everything else plain and let them talk. They make a white tee look like a decision.
shinrin: Aranya means forest. These are not forest green. They are Phirozi blue, the brightest thing on the rail, cut straight and easy. One colour, head to ankle. Wear them with white and nothing else needs to happen.
sora: Sara means sky: wide, open, no edges. Wide-leg trousers in cream cotton with a drawstring waist. They go with every piece in this collection. Buy these first. Build the rest around them.
devika: Devika means little goddess. A forest green layer in open net that lets everything underneath show through. It is barely there and it changes the whole outfit. Wear it over black, over white, over skin.
kiya: Kiya is the hour the light goes soft. Drawstring shorts in pale sage with a stitched, fringed hem. Loose in the leg and short enough to mean it. Made for heat, long walks and doing very little.
layla: Kiya is the hour the light goes soft. The same drawstring shorts in sky blue, cut from soft cotton. Loose in the leg, easy at the waist. The colour of the first ten minutes after sunset.
jing: Kiya is the hour the light goes soft. The same shorts in deep olive, cut from soft denim so they hold their shape. A little heavier, a little tougher. The pair to wear when sage feels too polite.
ekatva: Ektava means oneness. A white hooded poncho with fringed edges and stitching at every seam. It goes over everything and makes it one outfit. Hood up, arms free. The piece people ask about.
kora: Kora means pure, plain, untouched. An open hooded jacket in natural cotton with two deep pockets. No buttons, no lining, no noise. It is the layer you reach for without thinking and never regret.
amara: Swadhyaya means the study of the self. A short open jacket in ivory, cut square with wide sleeves that stop at the elbow. It sits on the shoulders like a frame. Everything under it looks more deliberate.
vasanta: Vasanta means spring. An open shrug in pale yellow linen, edged with black diamonds down the front. Cool, light and cut wide. The trim is the whole story: one line of pattern doing the work of a full print.
pema: Pema is the lotus, again, because it is worth saying twice. A long open layer in woven red and cream stripe, patterned cotton, cut to the calf. It hangs straight and swings wide. A coat for weather that does not need one.
